market microstructure.def: The mechanics by which orders become trades: the venues, the order book, the rules and the intermediaries that stand between an order and its fill.

round trip.def: Opening a position and later closing it, such as a buy followed by a sale. Trading costs are often quoted per round trip, since both legs pay them.

market capitalization.def: A company's share price times its number of shares: the value the market puts on the whole company.

public float.def: The shares of a company that are available to trade, leaving out those held by insiders, governments and other restricted holders.

index divisor.def: The number that the total float-adjusted market value of an index's companies is divided by to give the index level. The index provider adjusts it so that membership changes and similar events do not move the level.

spin-off.def: The separation of a subsidiary into a new, independent company, whose shares go to the parent company's shareholders.

ex-dividend date.def: The first day on which a buyer of a stock no longer receives its next dividend. The share price typically drops by about the dividend that morning.

price-return index.def: An index that tracks only price changes, so that dividends paid out by its companies lower its level. SPX is a price-return index.

total-return index.def: An index that adds back dividends as if they were reinvested, so that it tracks what a holder actually earned. SPTR is the total-return version of the S&P 500.

stock split.def: A change in the number of a company's shares with no change in its value, such as a 2-for-1 split that doubles the shares and halves the price.

exchange-traded fund.def: A fund whose shares trade on an exchange like a stock, usually built to track an index. Abbreviated ETF.

tick size.def: The smallest step in which a contract's price can change, such as a quarter of an index point for ES futures.

Section 1256 contract.def: A contract, such as a broad-based index option or a regulated futures contract, taxed under Section 1256 of the Internal Revenue Code. Its gains count as 60% long-term and 40% short-term whatever the holding period, and open positions are marked to market at the end of the year.

special opening quotation.def: The settlement value of AM-settled index options, built from the first reported trade of each component stock on the expiry morning. It can differ from every index level quoted that morning. Abbreviated SOQ.

circuit breaker.def: A rule that halts trading, across the whole market or in a single stock, after a large and fast price move.

physical settlement.def: Settling an option or future by delivering the underlying itself, such as 100 shares of SPY for each assigned contract, rather than cash.

covered call.def: A sold call option backed by owning the shares it may require you to deliver.

naked option.def: A sold option backed neither by the underlying nor by enough cash to meet the obligation, so that the seller's loss is limited only by how far the price can move.

buying power.def: The value of new positions that a margin account can open, given its equity and the broker's margin requirements.

regular trading hours.def: The main session of the American stock market, 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM Eastern Time. Abbreviated RTH.

futures basis.def: The difference between a futures price and the price of its underlying. For an index future it reflects interest and dividends until expiry, and it shrinks to zero at expiry.

SPAN margin.def: The risk-based margin system for futures and options on futures, developed by the CME, which sets the requirement from the worst loss across a set of price and volatility scenarios.

Regulation NMS.def: The SEC rules of 2005 for the National Market System, which require American equity trades to execute at or better than the National Best Bid and Offer and govern how venues are linked.

National Best Bid and Offer.def: The highest bid and the lowest offer displayed for a security across the registered exchanges at a given moment. Trades must execute at or inside it. Abbreviated NBBO.

Securities Information Processor.def: The regulated system that gathers quotes and trades from every American equity venue, computes the National Best Bid and Offer and publishes the consolidated tape. Abbreviated SIP.

price improvement.def: A fill at a better price than the National Best Bid and Offer on your side: below the best offer for a buy, or above the best bid for a sell.

lit exchange.def: A registered exchange that displays its order book publicly, so that its best bids and offers feed the National Best Bid and Offer.

dark pool.def: A trading venue that does not display its orders, run by a bank or broker. Its trades fill at or inside the public best bid and offer, often at the midpoint.

alternative trading system.def: The regulatory name for a trading venue that is not a registered exchange, such as a dark pool. Abbreviated ATS.

wholesaler.def: A trading firm that pays brokers for their retail orders and fills them from its own inventory, off the exchanges, at or inside the National Best Bid and Offer.

internalization.def: Filling a customer's order against the firm's own book instead of sending it to an exchange. A wholesaler that internalizes nets buyers against sellers and hedges only the difference.

payment for order flow.def: The payment a wholesaler makes to a broker for the right to fill that broker's customer orders. Abbreviated PFOF.

Rule 605.def: The SEC rule requiring every market center to publish monthly averages of its execution quality by order type, such as effective spread and price improvement.

Rule 606.def: The SEC rule requiring every broker to publish quarterly where it routed its customers' orders and what it was paid for them.

effective spread.def: Twice the distance between a fill price and the midpoint of the bid and ask when the order arrived: what the order paid, on the same scale as a quoted spread.

realized spread.def: Twice the distance between a fill price and the midpoint a short interval later: what the firm that filled the order kept after the price moved on.

making liquidity.def: Trading by resting an order on the book for others to trade against. The maker earns the spread, often receives a fee rebate, and risks being filled when the price is about to move against it.

taking liquidity.def: Trading by crossing the spread against orders already resting on the book. The taker gets an immediate fill and pays the spread and, usually, a fee.

order book.def: The live list of resting buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) for a security, arranged by price, with the quantity waiting at each level.

bid-ask bounce.def: The alternation of the last trade price between the bid and the ask as buyers and sellers arrive in turn. It adds noise and false mean reversion to any series of last prices.

walking the book.def: What a market order larger than the quantity at the best price does: it fills at the best level, then at each worse level in turn, until it is complete.

slippage.def: The gap between the price you expected or used as a reference, such as the best quote or the mid, and the average price you actually got.

maker-taker.def: The fee model of most American exchanges, which pays a small rebate to orders that rest on the book and charges a fee to orders that trade against them.

inverted market.def: An exchange that reverses the maker-taker model, paying orders that take liquidity and charging orders that rest on the book. Also called a subsidy market.

queue position.def: Where a resting limit order stands among the orders at the same price. Orders at a price fill in the order they arrived, so one at the back can wait while trades print at its price.

market order.def: An order to buy or sell at once at the best available prices. It promises a fill but not a price.

limit order.def: An order to buy at or below a stated price, or to sell at or above it. It promises the price but not a fill.

marketable limit order.def: A limit order priced at or through the current best quote on the other side, so that it fills at once in normal conditions but never beyond its limit.

immediate-or-cancel order.def: A limit order that fills whatever it can at once and cancels the rest instead of resting on the book. Abbreviated IOC.

market-on-close order.def: An order to trade at the official closing price, which the closing auction sets. Abbreviated MOC.

closing auction.def: The process in the last minutes of the American trading day in which the exchanges gather orders and fill them all at one price, the official close.

vertical spread.def: A position of two options of the same type on the same underlying and expiry, one bought and one sold at different strikes. A put spread is one kind.

legging.def: Entering or closing a multi-leg option position one leg at a time, as separate orders, which exposes you to price moves between the fills.

average daily volume.def: The number of shares or contracts of a security that trade on a typical day, averaged over a recent period. Abbreviated ADV.

iceberg order.def: A large limit order that shows only a small part of its size on the book at a time, replacing each part as it fills.

cash account.def: A brokerage account that trades only with settled cash and lends nothing, so it can never receive a margin call. Options sold in it must be covered by shares or by cash.

trade settlement.def: The actual exchange of cash and securities after a trade. American stocks and options settle one business day after the trade date, written T+1.

maintenance margin.def: The minimum equity, as a share of a position's value, that a margin account must keep after the purchase. Falling below it brings a margin call; under Regulation T it is 25% for stock.

pattern day trader.def: The regulatory label for a margin account under 25,000 dollars that makes four or more day trades in five trading days. Such an account is flagged and restricted.

long-term capital gain.def: A gain on a position held for more than a year, taxed at a lower rate than ordinary income.

short-term capital gain.def: A gain on a position held for a year or less, taxed at the ordinary income rate.

Net Investment Income Tax.def: A 3.8% federal surtax on the investment income, capital gains included, of higher-income American taxpayers. Abbreviated NIIT.

broad-based index.def: For the Section 1256 test, loosely, an index of 10 or more securities in which no single one exceeds 30% of the weight. Options on such an index can qualify for 60/40 tax treatment.

wash-sale rule.def: The tax rule that disallows a loss on a security if a substantially identical one is bought within 30 days before or after the sale. The loss is added to the new position's cost basis. It does not apply to Section 1256 contracts.

cost basis.def: The purchase price of a position for tax purposes, from which the taxable gain or loss on its sale is measured.
